summary: Explains how to connect IPv6 islands over an IPv4 MPLS core using IPv6 Provider Edge routers. Dual-stack edge routers exchange IPv6 reachability with BGP, so the core only has to run IPv4 MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 networks are like islands with an old IPv4 sea between them. 6PE builds boats at the shore, so IPv6 traffic crosses without changing the sea in the middle.

questions: how does ipv6 work over an ipv4 mpls core
what bgp next hop does 6pe use
subtitle: How an ISP can carry IPv6 across an IPv4-only MPLS core by upgrading only its edge routers.

tldr.problem: An ISP with an IPv4 MPLS network wants to offer IPv6 to customers without upgrading its core or configuring and maintaining explicit tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: Dual-stack IPv6 Provider Edge (6PE) routers exchange labeled IPv6 prefixes over MP-BGP running on IPv4, carry their IPv4 address as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 next hop, and forward IPv6 packets over ordinary IPv4-signaled LSPs using a two-label stack.
tldr.outcome: Only some edge routers need upgrading and the core stays IPv4 MPLS. The approach gives global IPv6 reachability, not IPv6 VPNs.

today: RFC 4798 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
The RFC lists three ways to give IPv6 connectivity over an MPLS core: IPv6-signaled LSPs, configured tunneling over IPv4-signaled LSPs, or the IPv6 Provider Edge (6PE) approach defined here. 6PE is meant for environments where all tunnels are set up dynamically and the effort of configuring and maintaining explicit tunnels is not acceptable.

The edge routers facing IPv6 islands must be dual-stack, MP-BGP-speaking routers, while core routers only need to run IPv4 MPLS. An IPv6 island is a network running native IPv6, such as a customer site connected through its Customer Edge (CE) router to a Provider Edge router.

No IPv4 headers are inserted in front of the IPv6 packets between customer and provider edge. The scope is global IPv6 reachability. IPv6 VPNs are out of scope and are covered by RFC 4659.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISP only has to change the shore stations. The big sea in the middle stays exactly as it is.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
A 6PE router sits on the border of the IPv4 MPLS cloud and MUST be dual-stack, with at least one IPv4 address on the core side and at least one IPv6 address on the customer side. The IPv4 address must be routable in the core and have a label bound to it by an IPv4 label distribution protocol. No extra routes need to be injected into the IPv4 cloud.

The router that receives IPv6 packets from a site is the ingress 6PE, and the one that forwards them to a site is the egress 6PE. There are two steps:

  • The 6PE routers exchange IPv6 prefixes over MP-BGP sessions running over IPv4, as in RFC 2545. The AFI MUST be IPv6 (value 2). The egress router's IPv4 address MUST be encoded as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address in the BGP Next Hop field. The 6PE MUST also bind a label to the prefix as per RFC 3107, using the label SAFI (value 4).
  • The ingress router MUST forward the IPv6 data over the IPv4-signaled LSP towards the egress router named by that next hop.

As BGP requires, PE routers form a full peering mesh unless route reflectors are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Shore stations tell each other which houses are on their island, and give their own sea address. To send a package, the first station looks up the destination's station and sends it along the existing sea route.

sections.title: Transport and Label Binding
sections.content:
The IPv4-signaled LSPs can be set up by any existing technique, such as LDP or RSVP-TE. To ensure interoperability, all 6PE implementations MUST support tunneling over LSPs established by LDP.

The ingress 6PE MUST impose labels directly onto the IPv6 packet, without first prepending an IPv4 header. The outer label MUST correspond to the IPv4-signaled LSP from ingress to egress.

A second label, bound to the IPv6 prefix by MP-BGP, MUST be used. It allows Penultimate Hop Popping on the router before the egress without that router needing any IPv6 support. It also lets an LSP that uses the IPv4 Explicit NULL label on its last hop carry IPv6, which a single label could not do. The egress may advertise an arbitrary label, which identifies an IPv6 routing context or outgoing interface, or the IPv6 Explicit Null Label. An ingress 6PE MUST be able to accept any such label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets two stickers. The outer one says which sea route to take. The inner one tells the last station that this is an IPv6 package.

sections.title: MTU Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 2460 requires every IPv6 link to have an MTU of 1280 octets or larger. So MPLS links used for 6PE that cannot fragment and reassemble on their own must be configured with an MTU of at least 1280 octets plus the encapsulation overhead.

To simplify Path MTU discovery, an administrator can set the MTU on the core-facing interfaces of the ingress 6PE consistent with the core MTU. The ingress can then send ICMP Packet Too Big messages without the packets entering the core. Otherwise, core routers can generate them using the mechanism in RFC 3032.

If a core link has an MTU below 1280 and receives a larger encapsulated packet, the Packet Too Big message may never reach the sender, and the sender sees data vanish without knowing why. This only happens if the MTU recommendation is not followed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every road in the IPv6 world has to fit a truck of a minimum size. If some sea route is narrower, the warning to turn back might get lost.

sections.title: Crossing Multiple Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
When the two IPv6 islands connect to different Autonomous Systems, the RFC describes three approaches, each equivalent to one in Section 10 of RFC 4364:

  • (a) The ASBR uses eBGP to pass unlabeled IPv6 routes to the neighbouring AS. No inter-AS LSPs are used, and each AS has its own mesh of LSPs. IPv6 must be active on the inter-ASBR links.
  • (b) The ASBR uses eBGP to pass labeled IPv6 routes. This needs LSPs across the ASes. The ASBRs may peer over IPv4 or IPv6.
  • (c) 6PE routers in different ASes set up multi-hop eBGP sessions over IPv4 and exchange labeled IPv6 routes, while ASBRs pass labeled IPv4 /32 routes to the 6PE routers. ASBRs need not be dual-stack, and IPv6 need not be active on inter-ASBR links.

In approach (c), exchange of IPv6 routes can only start after BGP has created IPv4 connectivity between the ASes.
sections.plainLanguage: When the sea belongs to several owners, there are three ways for them to pass along the island news, and each one asks a bit more or less of the owners.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says no new security issues are raised beyond those already in BGP-4 and the use of MP-BGP for IPv6, and the security features and policy of the ISP domain apply. Approach (a) adds nothing beyond eBGP for IPv6.

Approaches (b) and (c) need LSPs across AS boundaries, so appropriate trust must exist among the ASes on the path. To avoid label spoofing, an ASBR 6PE SHOULD only accept labeled packets from its peer if the topmost label is one it explicitly signaled to that peer.

In approach (c), label spoofing is harder to prevent, because the egress 6PE may be unable to check whether the label was pushed by an ingress 6PE allowed to do so. The same issue applies to option (c) in RFC 4364, and addressing it is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: If strangers can guess the right sticker, they might sneak packages in. Stations should only accept stickers they handed out themselves.
